channel.title: Sprawl — dev blog
channel.description: Stories from building Sprawl, an isometric open-world magic RPG.

item.title: Who comes to Oakwell?
item.description: Sprawl now opens on a title screen. You can shape the person who arrives, and the game shows you how what you do in Oakwell changes them.
item.content:encoded:
Who comes to Oakwell?

Sprawl now opens on a title screen. You can shape the person who arrives, and the game shows you how what you do in Oakwell changes them.

Until this week, launching Sprawl dropped you straight into Oakwell's square as the same hooded traveller every time. Now the game opens on a title. The square lies dimmed behind it, and there are three choices: Continue, New Game and Quit. Continue names who it will bring back and the day they had reached. With no saved character it is greyed out and says so, and nothing can select it.

A body of your own

New Game opens the character creator. Everyone in Sprawl is built from the same procedural body, shaped by sliders, so the creator gives you those same sliders: muscle, weight, height, shape and an age from 18 to 70, then skin, hair colour, red in the hair, a hair style and a beard. Six starting outfits are made from clothes already in the game, from the Forester's to the Pilgrim's, with a choice of head piece and cloak on top. The figure in the middle is drawn by the same renderer as the townsfolk, and you can turn it to see every side. Type a name or ask the dice, then choose Begin in Oakwell.

There is no class to pick. Your trade and your vows come later, from what you actually do in town. Every outfit keeps the traveller's oak staff, because the town's first fighting style is built on it. The arrival card then names you, and you walk out into the square as the person you made.

Oakwell is the same permanent town in every life, so New Game starts a new life in it rather than a new world. If a character already exists, the game asks before going on. Nothing is thrown away: the previous life's files are set aside in a folder of their own, with a note explaining how to bring them back.

Growth you can read

Rings around the health vial arrived a week ago, to show essence gathering as you live. Measured against Oakwell itself, they came too quickly at first and then stalled. Simulated players, run minute by minute without the game engine, were at ring eight within ten minutes and then had little left to earn. Each ring now has a minimum cost. A busy model player who does a bit of everything reaches the first ring in about two minutes and the first talent, at ring five, in about an hour. Walking alone takes around three hours to earn a ring.

Those are measurements of simulated players, not people. The first human sessions will show whether the pace feels right. Characters saved before the change keep every ring they had already reached; only the rings beyond them follow the new curve.

When something you do feeds you, a small caption over your head now names it, such as Trading feeding Bargain, Speak and Coin. Rings of a Life, the character sheet, now also lists what you have grown from lately, the vows you hold and which way they lean your next points, and the work you have taken up.

Room on the screen

The field journal on the right used to sit underneath the roads panel, which covered it and took its clicks. On a desktop screen the two now stack. On a small screen only one shows at a time: the journal during ordinary town life, and the road guide when something dangerous is close.

All of this was checked in the running game with automated keys and clicks, at three screen sizes. Equipment comes next, so that something you pick up in play can be worn, shown on your figure and saved.

item.title: Through the smoke
item.description: West of Oakwell, the trees now close over the path. In a woodcutters' clearing, an old stump has gone hollow, and smoke stands in the cleft at its foot.
item.content:encoded:
Through the smoke

West of Oakwell, the trees now close over the path. In a woodcutters' clearing, an old stump has gone hollow, and smoke stands in the cleft at its foot.

Leave Oakwell by the west gate and the path used to run between scattered oaks on a bright lawn. It read as a park, not a wood. That side of town is now an old wood: twisted oaks whose crowns meet overhead, young trees and undergrowth reaching out at the margin, and light breaking through the canopy in broad pools and small flecks.

None of it is placed by hand around Oakwell. The wood follows rules for woodland, read from the town's plan, so another town with a wood beside it would grow its own. The path stays readable, with no old oak standing too close in front of it. Up to three sunlit glades open off it. The wood also carries on past the edge you can walk to, so the far side is more trees rather than lawn and then nothing. Trunks, boulders and fallen logs block your way; ferns let you through.

The colours took the most work. Oakwell's final colour grade deepens shadow and lifts colour across the whole picture, and the first attempt at the wood came out with black crowns and a mustard floor. Its colours are now chosen so that the graded picture matches the reference painting. An image review against that painting scored the view outside the gate 3.5 out of 10 before and 6.5 after. It also named what is still missing: the upper canopy still reads partly as a carpet of rounded crowns, and the boulders are the shared grey stones used elsewhere.

The stump in the clearing

A short walk off the path, an old oak's stump stands hollow at the heart. A slow swirl of dark green smoke stands upright in the cleft at its foot. It is the first dungeon you can walk into from Oakwell. In Sprawl, dungeons are other realities, and their entrances form in ordinary things behind a veil of smoke.

Walk into the smoke, press E beside it, or click the stump. The veil rolls out until it fills the screen, a card names the place, and you step out of a matching opening on the other side: the Teeming Barrow, a root hollow.

Packed loam and moss lie underfoot, living roots bind the earth walls, and glowcaps give the only light. Rooms reveal themselves only as you see them. Rootlings, barkback beetles and spore toads wait in them, and the Rootmother waits in the sanctum. Each one marks its blow on the ground before it lands, so you can step aside. You fight them with the same controls as in town: strike, hold for a heavy blow, dodge, and use your abilities. Badly hurt, they break off and run.

What they leave behind is what they were: living root, glowcaps, bark carapace, mandibles, toad skin, spore sacs and heartwood. Nothing pays coin. Root-wrapped hoards hold the realm's shards. Walk back to the hollow trunk you came through to step out onto the same spot in the wood. If you are beaten down inside, the smoke throws you back out.

The dungeon, your bag and the side of the veil you were on are saved together. Continue reopens the game inside or outside, wherever you stopped.

Two pieces that had to meet

The wood and the dungeon were built side by side, and trying them together found a problem. The new wood grew so dense that no open ground was left near the walls, so the stump moved to a spot 43 metres out in the far south-west. The clearing rule now fells the few trees whose crowns would hide the stump from the camera, leaving their plain stumps behind. The entrance now stands about 16 metres from the walls, a short walk from the west gate.

This is a first slice: one realm, at its first depth. The rules already know other kinds of entrance, such as an old door in a wall or a cave mouth, but only the stump stands in Oakwell. Deeper levels and the rest of the dungeon plan are still to come. Both pieces were checked in the running game with automated walks, keys and clicks. Neither has had a human playtest yet.

item.title: Fruit, stone, grain and a mill
item.description: Fallen fruit, a quartz seam, a blocked road and a watermill: Oakwell's everyday work is starting to answer what the town actually needs.
item.content:encoded:
Fruit, stone, grain and a mill

Fallen fruit, a quartz seam, a blocked road and a watermill: Oakwell's everyday work is starting to answer what the town actually needs.

Windfalls

The orchard east of Oakwell used to have fallen fruit painted on its grass. Now it is real. Walk up to a windfall apple or pear, press E, and that one piece goes into your satchel. Each fallen fruit has its own place in the orchard, and the game remembers when it is gone, so it stays gone after you quit and Continue. A full bag leaves the fruit where it lay.

Picking from the crowns, ripening through the seasons, pressing and orchard workers are all still ahead.

Reading the rock

Mining the outcrops beyond the town now teaches judgement through the work itself. After three successful strikes, you can tell whether an exposed seam still holds mineral or only stone. After six strikes across three outcrops, you can also judge how many workable strikes it has left.

The herb bag's Work and professions page now sets out the livelihoods ahead. It lists twenty-five of them, in twenty-three families. Three ordinary ones work today: gathering plants, preparing them, and mining. The rest are shown as planned, so you can see where the work is going. Everyday skills stay open to everyone, while your one major profession still unlocks the deeper methods.

A road to clear

Odette at the inn is running low on grain. Wenna, the travelling merchant, can tell you why: a storm has brought timber down across her reserve beside the east road. You can go and look, buy a pick from Wenna's own limited stock, and work at the blockage. Clearing it pays nothing by itself. Wenna's cart then has to make the real journey, carrying six measures at a time from a reserve of 48, and the inn buys only what its till can afford. Odette brews with it on her next working day, and households can buy the same grain with their own money.

The reserve does not refill. When it runs dry, the shortage stays visible until the wider county's trade reaches Oakwell, which is separate work still to come.

The mill keeps turning

Grinding dried herbs by hand, or brewing remedies successfully, now teaches something new: Repeat, an understanding of motion that does the same thing again. Once you have learned enough of it, you can build a herb grinder at Oakwell's watermill from two branches and a piece of iron ore. Load it with up to eight real dried plant parts and walk away. Each part takes fifteen minutes of game time, and the powder waits in the tray, keeping where it came from, its quality and any doubt about which plant it was. The mill supplies motion, not ingredients, so an empty grinder makes nothing.

The first time the grinder finishes a part on its own, you learn Automation, once. After that it keeps producing goods without teaching you anything more. Copying and duplication, the next steps along that branch, come later. The mill was accepted before its complete in-game run had finished, so the whole sequence of learning, building, grinding and coming back after Continue still needs that final check.

item.title: When the house wakes
item.description: Quiet footsteps can leave a sleeping household undisturbed. A broken pantry crock gives its owner something to investigate.
item.content:encoded:
When the house wakes

3 November 2026

Quiet footsteps can leave a sleeping household undisturbed. A broken pantry crock gives its owner something to investigate.

The first property encounter gave an Oakwell resident a reason to care about her home and provisions. This follow-up gives that same household a way to hear what is happening while its owner sleeps.

Move softly

The existing walk control now matters near the cottage. Slower walking makes softer footfalls than running or sprinting. The same choice is available from a touch button. Footsteps follow the ground you actually cover, so pushing against a wall does not produce an endless stream of contacts.

A careful visitor can enter through the real doorway, inspect the unlocked chest and deliberately take an apple while the owner remains asleep. Ownership still applies. The absence of a witness leaves the culprit unidentified.

An opened chest still contains owned food. Taking an apple is a separate choice.

A crash changes the night

Breaking the pantry crock produces a pottery crash. Walls reduce the sound, and distance matters. A sufficiently loud sound can make the resident stir, wake and walk toward its approximate origin.

A loud mistake changes the household's response, even when playback is muted.

She follows the same floors and routes as the town's ordinary residents. A piece of furniture in the way remains an obstacle. She needs a reachable place from which to look around, and one noise cannot send her searching forever.

Her response follows the information available. A sound gives her a direction and a reason to investigate. Seeing a new act can identify someone. Finding broken pottery can establish damage. The crash itself does not supply the name of the person who caused it.

That distinction keeps stealth meaningful. An owner can wake, find a loss and still have no supported claim against the player. Current intruders can also be noticed and warned once she is awake. She addresses that intrusion first, while the earlier noise can remain unexplained.

Discovering damaged provisions supplies a loss, rather than the name of a culprit.

Continue the same moment

Saving during the stir preserves her position, the pending wake and the time already spent. Continuing resumes that response. It does not replay the crash or grant a fresh delay before she wakes.

Part of a footstep survives too. Repeatedly saving and loading between contacts cannot keep granting another silent stretch of floor. If an old response has already expired, continuing respects that elapsed time.

Sound detection also works with playback muted. Turning down the game's audio changes what the player hears; the people in the world still respond to events around them.

One household, proved further

The checks follow a controlled night in the existing cottage, then continue from a saved stir in a new game process. They exercise ordinary controls and resident navigation, with a disclosed clock setup so the result can be reproduced.

This remains a bounded encounter. Real closable doors and locks, a placed sound-suppression rune, travelling reports and guard pursuit are further stages. The current step makes a quiet visit and a noisy mistake produce different, understandable consequences in the same home.

item.title: Someone lives here
item.description: One Oakwell household now has a reason to care when you walk through its door, open its chest or break its provisions.
item.content:encoded:
Someone lives here

3 November 2026

One Oakwell household now has a reason to care when you walk through its door, open its chest or break its provisions.

A house becomes more interesting when the person living there has something to say about your visit. This review build begins with one of Oakwell's existing residents and her actual cottage, reached through the same doorway you can already walk through.

There is a private chest containing three apples and an earthenware pantry pot holding two rolls. Small possessions, but they belong to someone.

A chance to leave

If a resident notices you entering the private room, you receive a clear warning and time to leave through the door. Leaving ends that immediate warning. No stolen goods or fight appear merely because you crossed a threshold.

Staying after the warning, or repeatedly returning after being recognised, earns a firmer response. Recognition matters: an anonymous visitor cannot accumulate a secret repeat-offender record in someone's mind.

Opening is a choice. Taking is another.

The chest first offers inspection. Opening its lid reveals the apples and a separately labelled Steal action. Keyboard, mouse and touch all make that choice explicit. Holding down an old inspection click while the lid opens cannot quietly turn its release into theft.

The pantry pot can be broken. Its shards and provisions stay in the cottage; collecting a roll is another deliberate action. A full satchel leaves the food where it is. Repeated input cannot produce more apples, rolls or broken pots.

What the resident knows

The owner can object to damage or theft she actually witnesses. Her sight depends on where she is, where she is looking and the walls between you. Being elsewhere in Oakwell does not tell her what happened at home.

An unnoticed theft can succeed. Later, when she reaches the chest and finds food missing, she can discover the loss without discovering the thief. The player standing nearby does not become guilty by proximity.

For a witnessed loss, a visible compensation offer transfers real coins from your purse to hers. Paying settles the known loss once. She still remembers the incident, and her conversation reflects whether you have paid. An unidentified loss produces no bill for the player.

Coming back preserves the consequence

The open lid, broken pottery, remaining food, carried items, warnings and witness memory are saved together. Continuing keeps the same household history. Older characters gain the new household state through a versioned migration while retaining their existing belongings and progress.

This is the first bounded encounter in a larger property and crime design. Sound propagation and waking sleepers, real locks, a placed sound-suppression rune, physical reports to guards and pursuit remain further stages. The current encounter proves private space, deliberate taking and responses grounded in what a resident can know.

The recorded checks use controlled resident positions and a fixed clock to make the comparison reproducible in the running town. Human playtesting still needs to establish whether the warning, ownership and consequences are clear without an explanation beside them.

item.title: Room between the sunflowers
item.description: A garden path should still look like somewhere you can walk. The sunflowers had been keeping their own rules: broad leaves, tall yellow heads and a carpet of little red flowers could grow straight across a lane.
item.content:encoded:
Room between the sunflowers

3 November 2026

A garden path should still look like somewhere you can walk. The sunflowers had been keeping their own rules: broad leaves, tall yellow heads and a carpet of little red flowers could grow straight across a lane.

They now leave room for the whole plant. The low flowers respect that space too, so clearing the stalks does not leave a second carpet hiding the route. Raised planters keep their flowers when the complete plant fits inside the rim.

This is a controlled bed rendered with the game's Core renderer, using the same seed, camera and light. It is not a gameplay capture. The flowers keep their familiar shapes; the difference is the space between them.

Native review at ordinary play zoom remains ahead, including the older Wainscross garden work. This change checks the geometry around lanes, doorways, gates and stairs; it does not yet establish how a moving player reads every garden.

item.title: From leaf to draught
item.description: An unfamiliar plant is a small mystery. A carefully made remedy is a reason to carry it home.
item.content:encoded:
From leaf to draught

An unfamiliar plant is a small mystery. A carefully made remedy is a reason to carry it home.

Oakwell's herbalism work already gave a gathered plant a place in your bag and a name in your own words. It remembered what you tasted and what a herbalist told you. This review takes the next step: choosing a useful part, preparing it at the cauldron and leaving with a draught you can actually use.

The pictures come from automated input in the actual town. Daylight and the herbalist's work pause are held for the review; the plants, routes, payment and earned practice come from ordinary play controls.

A process you can learn

The first recipe asks for an identified woundwort leaf or flower. A tempting folk name is not enough. You still need to gather the specimen, keep it and learn what it is before turning it into medicine.

At the cauldron, cutting preserves quality while crushing extracts more quickly. The vessel matters too. Warm the solvent, watch for steam, add the prepared herb and give the colour time to spread. Stir gently, strain and bottle.

Those actions leave a history. An early addition, too much stirring or a hard boil can weaken the result. A badly scorched batch can be ruined. Reopening the bag does not give the same ingredients another chance to roll a better outcome.

A bottle keeps the story of its making: the part's condition, how hot the liquid was when it went in, the extraction, the stirring and any scorching. If one batch is weaker than another, there is a cause to find and a decision to try differently next time.

Useful before a title

You do not need a profession to begin. Successful gathering and preparation count while you are still deciding what kind of craftsperson to become. The first useful draught can restore the same health you risk out in the town's dangers.

The permanent choice comes later. One major vocation gives a character a direction, while ordinary skills stay open. After six real harvests, the Herbalist can choose Gentle hand to recover extra usable material, or Field preservation to carry viable fresh ingredients further into preparation. At fifteen, a second choice deepens that method. From stem to salve carries careful handling into stronger remedies; another refinement puts more into the harvest itself.

The choice explains what will change before you confirm it. Reading the alternatives earns nothing, and choosing one passes over the other. The reward is a different way to work with the next real ingredient.

To reach the second choice, the review uses the ordinary dawn-wait menu, lets four actual midnights pass and returns to the regrown plants. Fifteen real harvests earn the refinement. The next recorded draught restores nine health; that same ingredient and brewing history would restore seven without the chosen refinement.

Coming back to your work

The plant, its spent part, the active brew, your practice and the remaining doses belong to one saved character. The review restarts the game with a batch left halfway through, finishes it, then restarts again with the bottled dose still carried.

Drinking that dose restores the four missing health and removes it from the roll. Its full strength is seven, but it only heals what is missing. Trying to use the same dose again grants nothing, and another restart keeps it spent.

That is the shape of a complete profession session: go looking, notice something, learn, prepare and come back with help you made yourself. It gives a quiet day in Oakwell a useful destination.

The review evidence distinguishes automated rule checks and declared native fixtures from an uncoached human session. The wider playtest still needs people to tell us whether these cues are clear and whether the choices feel worth making.

item.title: A reason to return
item.description: A journey becomes more interesting when what you learn changes what you take on the next one.
item.content:encoded:
A reason to return

A journey becomes more interesting when what you learn changes what you take on the next one.

Reddish grit catches in an outcrop outside Oakwell. More has washed through the grated outfall. The colour might suggest copper, but that is only a hypothesis. A conversation with the smith gives the weight and texture a meaning: iron ore, exposed in the old service passage below the well.

This expedition experiment joins places and actions already in Oakwell. There is a person to ask, a reason to prepare, a place to investigate and something useful to bring home. The smith does not lend you an invisible tool. A pick comes from Wenna's finite stock, and Edric's climbing supplies provide a safe way down.

You can also find the seam before noticing either surface sign. Examining the exposed rock records what you saw, giving you a question to take back to the smith. The journey can begin with a discovery below the well, followed by preparation and a return visit.

This isolated review scene stages the gear and route to check the discovery itself. Identification is supplied later for the test, as the caption declares. It checks the interaction with a stand-in traveller. Ordinary town playtesting remains pending.

What earns its place in the bag?

The seam yields iron ore and rough stone. Both need room in the satchel. You can work more of the small reserve, leave it for another visit, or turn back with what you have. Two rough stone can become a mortar and pestle through the existing bag action. Ore can answer a real workshop request when the smith has one open.

Two smaller discoveries sit along the dry walkway. A scoured gully makes the moving water worth noticing; maintenance scratches explain another way back to daylight. Neither is a compulsory stop. An optional itinerary organises the same observations, while contextual notes let you keep your own intentions.

The field notes begin with what you have actually noticed. Finding a clue gives the book a hypothesis to hold; asking about it adds a reason to choose particular tools. The optional itinerary follows that growing knowledge. Opening the book before setting out leaves the discovery yours to make.

One history to come home to

Connecting the journey exposed a less visible problem: the old underground save could restore a different copy of the traveller's belongings. Journey progress now joins the character's saved history, so ore, a worked seam and the way home travel together. Incompatible older histories are kept for recovery.

The book keeps the memory of the material you recovered after you have shaped it or handed it over. Its notes follow the history of the trip as your belongings change.

The automated checks cover finite resources, a full bag, repeated inputs and restored progress. An earlier scripted journey used ordinary Oakwell controls to ask the smith, buy the pick, return with materials and shape the stone into a mortar. A fresh process restored the same belongings and the worked seam. This remains an experiment awaiting uncoached testers. The full county connection, phone-scale review and session pacing still need their own evidence. The question for that first outing is simple: did finding something make you want to come back?

item.title: When the hammer stops
item.description: A town starts to feel alive when its people have reasons to stop what they are doing.
item.content:encoded:
When the hammer stops

A town starts to feel alive when its people have reasons to stop what they are doing.

That matters for Sprawl's first proper playtests. Gathering, trade and fighting need to fit into the same place. If a resident keeps working or chatting while a fight approaches, the town stops being convincing at exactly the moment it should become interesting.

The first implementation for this milestone gives Oakwell's residents a local response to nearby fighting. They need to see an active threat, at a sensible distance and height. A peaceful guard is still a peaceful guard. A fight on the other side of town does not magically tell everyone to go home.

An alarm interrupts the resident's work and conversation. They try to reach their own mapped home through the town's actual doorways. The route also has to keep clear of the danger they observed. If the shortest path is unsafe, they look for a longer way around. Someone already too close can move away; an apparently convenient path through the attacker is refused.

There is no promise of a safe route every time. If the way is blocked, the resident pauses and tries again. They are never moved through a wall or placed inside a house to make the result look right.

Getting indoors does not erase the rest of their life. Their scheduled destination and unfinished work stay attached to them. After a short period without another observation, they can return to what the current hour calls for. If their day changed while they were away, they follow that newer routine.

Conversation does not freeze the fight. A threat can approach while someone is talking, and the interruption releases both people to act. After sustained quiet, a small speech bubble offers the unfinished conversation again. The player chooses whether to return. Any offer of a service is checked afresh.

The native rehearsal now covers interruption, the walk home, return to work and choosing to pick up the conversation. Equipped defence and remembered protection remain later work. The next wider proof is a connected outing: learn what someone needs, prepare, venture out, return with something useful, and see the result survive leaving and coming back.

item.title: The same faces, different days
item.description: Oakwell should be somewhere you can recognise. A different adventure should not require Ysolde to become a different person, or a familiar road to lead to a town that has moved overnight.
item.content:encoded:
The same faces, different days

Oakwell should be somewhere you can recognise. A different adventure should not require Ysolde to become a different person, or a familiar road to lead to a town that has moved overnight.

The next implementation for review begins to separate the setting from the history that happens there. The county definition keeps its twelve settlements, their streets, rivers and main road connections. Highbury keeps its place too, even though its layout began as a generator experiment. Countryside details can still vary around those anchors.

The same distinction reaches Oakwell's three established residents. New histories start with the same Ysolde, Hamon and Odette, including their starting natures. Their choices can still respond to different circumstances. Familiarity gives those differences someone to happen to.

An existing history deserves the same care. Older saves keep the people they started with, including their original personalities. Remembered help, changed households, losses and belongings must survive Continue. The starting definition is not permission to wind a person's life back to the beginning.

There is still a seam to finish. Oakwell's compound inn and the separate town launches have older layout and save rules. Those need a careful transition before the entire setting can be called permanent in ordinary play. The other towns also need real resident lives behind the figures already standing in them.

This is a foundation for a day in Oakwell, not that whole day delivered. The next proof is a connected journey: notice a need, prepare, leave town, return and see what changed. Then close the game, come back, and find that the day still mattered.

item.title: A place to come back to
item.description: Oakwell will be there when you begin again. The question is what will happen to its people this time.
item.content:encoded:
A place to come back to

2 November 2026

Oakwell will be there when you begin again. The question is what will happen to its people this time.

We have made a decision about the kind of world Sprawl is becoming. Oakwell and its neighbouring towns will be recurring places in the game, with recognisable streets, working buildings and a core cast of familiar people. Marlbury belongs to that setting too.

Until now, the plan treated the first county as the place to prove a method for generating entirely different towns. Those tools are still useful. But the county itself is becoming somewhere worth keeping.

Familiar faces, different circumstances

Knowing a place gives its changes weight. You can learn where the mill stands, who works there and which road brings grain into town. When something goes wrong, you have a reason to notice.

The aim is for different stories to grow from the same people and consistent rules. A shortage, an unsafe road or your own decision to help can change what someone does next. Their response should follow what they need, what they know and what has actually happened.

These are possibilities we need to prove through play. They are not promises that every one of those situations is already working.

Keeping the cast does not mean freezing their lives. Supported changes during a game should remain changed: a move, a lost friendship, a closed workplace or a remembered kindness. Starting again begins a new history. Continuing a save keeps the history you made.

The land between the towns

There is still room for countryside to vary between new games. Woodland detail, minor trails, resources and suitable rural buildings can come from a saved seed. Once you find somewhere, it must remain there when you return.

The geography has responsibilities. The mill needs its river. A fishing village needs its shore. Roads must still reach their bridges and town entrances. Variation has to respect those connections and blend naturally into the surrounding land.

We also want each settlement to earn its own appearance. Climate, local materials, trade and terrain should shape its buildings and streets. Making Oakwell convincing does not finish the work of making a different architectural family convincing.

First, a day in Oakwell

The next useful milestone is a connected session of roughly half an hour to three quarters of an hour. You notice a real need, prepare for an outing, leave town, face or avoid danger, and return to see what your choice changed.

There must be a way back from a setback, and saving and continuing must preserve the result. The people around you need readable responses to what happens, including a sensible reaction when danger interrupts their day.

We will begin with Oakwell and its nearby countryside. That is enough to test whether the journey holds together. A neighbouring town comes after that; finishing every settlement and biome is not a condition for learning from the first session.

Before inviting trusted testers, the same journey also needs a dependable desktop package, clear controls, tested recovery and measured performance on the intended hardware. A successful automated check alone cannot tell us whether someone knows what to do or cares about the outcome.

This update sets the direction and the work ahead. It does not announce a finished playtest build. The goal is a place you can learn, people you can remember, and consequences that give you a reason to come back.

item.title: The quiet work counts
item.description: Gathering a plant should be part of a character's life, even before they choose a profession.
item.content:encoded:
The quiet work counts

Gathering a plant should be part of a character's life, even before they choose a profession.

Oakwell was remembering successful harvests for the Herbalist commitment, but the ordinary practice behind those acts was missing. A successful pick now teaches through the existing plant-handling rules as well. Handling the herb matters alongside the tending and cutting involved in taking it.

Your major profession remains a separate choice. These everyday gains happen while you are undecided and continue after committing. Repeated work grows familiar, following the same rules as other everyday practice.

A full satchel is an unsuccessful harvest. The part stays on the plant, and the failed attempt earns neither ordinary practice nor progress toward a profession. Locating or looking at a plant does not count as picking it.

Returning to Oakwell keeps the gathered specimens, the harvest history and that ordinary learning in the same character. Knowing more through work does not magically settle a doubtful plant name.

Special harvest methods and the Apothecary's remedies still have their own work ahead. This pass makes the small work already in the town count toward the person doing it.

item.title: Less work between footsteps
item.description: A village becomes more demanding as its people find work, return home and thread their way through narrow doors. Making that cheaper should leave their journeys intact.
item.content:encoded:
Less work between footsteps

1 November 2026

A village becomes more demanding as its people find work, return home and thread their way through narrow doors. Making that cheaper should leave their journeys intact.

This performance pass follows two small costs that happen often.

Choose an approach before checking every alternative

A worker needs to reach the actual anvil, hearth or serving place. Nearby furniture can leave enough room for their body while putting their feet outside the wider travel grid.

The router already handles that distinction. It previously swept every nearby approach for both ends of the journey before choosing one. It now considers the same approaches in the same order and checks them as they become useful. The chosen journey still gets its final physical safety check.

Stop leaving rubbish at every footfall

Walking across terraced ground checks the ground beneath the body and around its rim. Those checks also decide whether a bridge keeps feet dry, a landing enters water, or a stair connects two floors.

Some of those tiny checks created temporary objects on every stride. Direct loops now apply the same rules without those repeated allocations. The shoreline, stair heights and collision margins stay the same.

Measure the work, keep the journey

The comparison runs the original and revised movement code over identical generated towns, terraced towns and deliberate awkward cases. It checks exact route points and movement results before recording costs.

Across three generated towns, a batch of 64 journeys needed about half as many physical collision samples. In the four actual terraced-town fixtures, 256 short walks stopped creating roughly 1.8 to 1.9 million temporary managed bytes.

These are measurements of the movement systems running without the game engine. They establish less repeated work and less temporary memory; they do not establish a new frame rate on a phone. Full moving-town measurements remain the next check.

item.title: Flowers and footsteps
item.description: The little things at the edge of a street do a surprising amount of work. A bed of daisies, a spray of lavender and a patch of kitchen herbs ought to tell different stories before you stop to inspect them.
item.content:encoded:
Flowers and footsteps

The little things at the edge of a street do a surprising amount of work. A bed of daisies, a spray of lavender and a patch of kitchen herbs ought to tell different stories before you stop to inspect them. This pass gives the gardens in Sprawl's layered traced towns more recognisable shapes, and makes their planting leave room for the people passing by.

These are reproducible pictures from the game's Core renderer, rather than screenshots of a running Godot game. Each pair uses the same seed, camera and light. They show the geometry that the traced town renderer builds; a walk through the game remains a separate review.

A flower has a shape

The earlier daisies were little white discs on sticks. They now have separate petals around a warm centre. Lavender has branching stems, narrow leaves and small tiers of flowers, with gaps between them. Rosemary keeps its upright leafy form without borrowing lavender's purple flowers.

The extra detail is concentrated in deliberate garden beds. Broad meadow scatter keeps its simpler flower heads, so a small border does not set the cost of an entire field.

Room around the roots

A shrub can stand beside a path and still spread across it. Placement now allows for the whole plant: the offset lobes of a bush, its flowers, the fan of a herb spray and the lean of a grass tuft. Wider plants step back farther from lanes, doorways and stairs. Gateways also reserve an approach when there is no painted path to mark one.

This changes the scenery placed beside a route. It does not change the route itself or add new obstacles to walking.

Flowers inside the stone rim

The comparison in Wainscross exposed another small but visible fault. The paving of the square continued underneath the raised planter around its tree. The planting rules saw that paving and refused to grow flowers there, leaving an empty bed of soil.

A raised planter can now keep its flowers when their full spread fits inside its stone rim, even when a road is drawn beneath it in the town plan. The surrounding approaches remain protected. An ordinary bed at ground level still cannot grow over the square.

The next visual review is a walk through these gardens at the usual play zoom, checking the person against the flowers and the paths between them. Larger questions about woodland composition, orchard crowns and Oakwell's separate authored planting remain work for their own passes.

item.title: Finding your own map notes
item.description: A field book becomes useful when you can return to what you wrote. In the county map, a note can now bring its own patch of surveyed ground back into the local sketch.
item.content:encoded:
Finding your own map notes

A field book becomes useful when you can return to what you wrote. In the county map, a note can now bring its own patch of surveyed ground back into the local sketch.

Select an annotation and choose Locate, or press G while reading the map. The sketch centres on that pin and returns to a readable local scale. Your traveller stays where they are.

A copied page keeps its own annotations. Locate follows the selected note on the page you are reading; it does not switch you back to the original book or change either page's wording.

Typing stays typing. The shortcut cannot pull the map away while you are writing, and an empty page has no location to follow. Locating a pin does not discover new ground, improve your drawing hand or walk the road for you.

This adds a small return path through a growing notebook: write what matters, explore elsewhere, then find that mark again.

item.title: Finding the rhythm
item.description: A quick jab, a step away, another opening. A fight has a rhythm even before a spell enters it. The next town combat pass gives that rhythm a small, visible memory.
item.content:encoded:
Finding the rhythm

A quick jab, a step away, another opening. A fight has a rhythm even before a spell enters it. The next town combat pass gives that rhythm a small, visible memory.

Consecutive landed actions now build a count above the target. The second link shows a brass two, then three, then four. The lettering grows a little brighter and larger as the run continues, with a limit so a long exchange does not cover the fight.

An opening is worth keeping

The count follows successful actions. A bare-handed jab counts just as a staff strike or a spell does. Catching several small slimes with one action still gives one link: the number is a memory of the fighter's rhythm, rather than a tally of bodies caught in a sweep.

There is a short space to find the next opening. After about a second and a fifth without a landing, the run ends. Taking damage breaks it too. A successful dodge or parry keeps the run alive, so answering a threat can belong to the same exchange as pressing forward.

Opening a peaceful menu pauses that little clock. So does the brief pause that gives a landed blow its weight. The count belongs to the fight's own time.

First, make the rhythm readable

This is a feedback pass. The count does not yet make a blow stronger, and casting does not spend it on a magical finisher. Those are later steps: the town first needs to show clearly what continued a run and what broke it.

There is something satisfying about seeing a small sequence take shape. It gives the existing punches, weapons and spells a shared thread, while leaving their costs, reach and consequences where they already belong.

item.title: Choosing the Herbalist's path
item.description: Picking a plant is a small act. Doing it again, and returning with another carefully wrapped part, begins to look like a practice.
item.content:encoded:
Choosing the Herbalist's path

Picking a plant is a small act. Doing it again, and returning with another carefully wrapped part, begins to look like a practice.

Oakwell now remembers successful plant harvests as part of your character. Open the herbalist's bag with H to see that history. Failed attempts do not advance it, and reading the bag does not turn uncertainty into a certain plant name.

After three successful harvests, you can consider becoming a Herbalist. The first choice explains the commitment. A separate confirmation makes it permanent: one major profession, with no retraining. Closing the bag leaves you undecided.

A profession is not permission to touch a plant. Ordinary gathering remains open before and after the choice. A Herbalist can keep gathering, and the next successful harvest still counts.

Returning to the town keeps that earned history, the chosen identity and the specimens themselves together. That history belongs to the same saved character as your belongings.

This is the first native commitment step. Special harvest techniques and the Apothecary's remedy work still have their own work ahead.

item.title: Keeping checks where they belong
item.description: A village should spend its time on people moving, working and talking. Sometimes a performance improvement comes from finding work that belongs in the workshop instead.
item.content:encoded:
Keeping checks where they belong

1 November 2026

A village should spend its time on people moving, working and talking. Sometimes a performance improvement comes from finding work that belongs in the workshop instead.

Each time the town placed its people for drawing, it also checked whether every awake, visible resident was standing legally. That extra check recorded mistakes for our acceptance tests. The walking and routing systems already made their own collision decisions; this second pass did not move anyone or prevent a step.

The proposal keeps that full audit in every self-test and makes it available as an explicit diagnostic mode. Ordinary play can leave out the extra pass. Conversations, visibility, facing, walking, work and the pictures people paint keep the same paths.

A useful reduction with a clear limit

The comparison runs the real presentation routine with a recording graphics interface and real generated-town collision queries. It checks groups of sixteen, forty and one hundred people across three town plans, alternating the original and proposed code.

The recorded placement batches took about twenty-two to twenty-nine percent less CPU time. A batch of 256 placements for one hundred people stopped making 25,600 extra diagnostic queries. Both versions allocated no temporary managed memory in those warm batches.

These are component measurements on a shared desktop server. They are not game frames, a new phone frame rate or a promise that the whole town is that much faster. The normal engine acceptance tests have now passed. These measurements still do not establish a whole-game frame-rate gain.

The tests still have their eyes open

The test fixture deliberately supplies illegal footing. Every self-test, explicit audit and comparison mode still detects it. A moving and sleeping resident trace also keeps the same presentation states as the original routine.

The aim is to keep the checks that protect the game, and stop asking ordinary play to run a test-only audit over and over.

item.title: A traveller should come back whole
item.description: A traveller leaves Oakwell with a few apples, a half-healed wound and something new in their almanac. On returning, all three should belong to the same moment.
item.content:encoded:
A traveller should come back whole

A traveller leaves Oakwell with a few apples, a half-healed wound and something new in their almanac. On returning, all three should belong to the same moment.

That sounds obvious. It becomes less simple as a little town grows into a game. The satchel and its money had learned to travel with the town's workshops, deliveries and clock. Abilities, health and discoveries had their own history. Both could be correct on their own while remembering different moments.

One journey, one memory

This pass brings those histories under one character save. The community still owns the real goods and money. The learning book still owns abilities, health and discoveries. Earned profession choices have a place alongside them. Saving gathers those existing records into one complete document, checks it, then replaces the previous character file in one step.

Loading follows the same rule. First read everything into detached candidates. Check the town and world, each record's version, the character's floor and stair, the finite resources and the earned choices. Only after those checks agree does the traveller step back into the town.

An unreadable section protects the entire saved character. It does not load the apples first and discover a problem with health afterward. Older separate files are read together when no character save exists, and are kept after the new save is written.

Why this comes before the profession menu

Herbalism is where the boundary matters most. Tasting an unfamiliar leaf already connects a consumed specimen, a remembered sensation and the character's health. Those changes now have the same save boundary. A future remedy will need that same care: its healing must travel with the ingredient it consumed.

The profession rules already describe practice, a deliberate commitment and earned methods. This change makes room for those choices without giving the satchel a second owner or replacing the almanac with an older record. The full profession interface and its playable preparation loop remain work to do.

Bringing the old scene a little closer to retirement

The next pass removes the retired scene's duplicate fishing adapter. Town fishing already has its own real banks, float, catch decision and journal. Keeping a second scene implementation meant keeping another set of prompts, input hooks and tests alive after the act had moved home.

The fish ecology and fishing rules stay. The playable town stays. The obsolete scene adapter goes, with the town's existing angling journey serving as the verification gate.

A world can grow through new places and new actions. Sometimes it also needs a careful pass through the joins, so that the next thing we add has somewhere dependable to belong.

item.title: A mortar in Oakwell
item.description: A dried leaf is still a leaf until you do something with it. Oakwell now has another small act of preparation: carrying a mortar and pestle lets you grind a dried plant part in the herbalist's bag.
item.content:encoded:
A mortar in Oakwell

A dried leaf is still a leaf until you do something with it. Oakwell now has another small act of preparation: carrying a mortar and pestle lets you grind a dried plant part in the herbalist's bag.

The action uses one actual part. The mortar stays with you, the powder takes its place among your belongings, and successful grinding contributes to the character's existing practice. Wenna already carries a finite mortar and a few uncertain dried specimens, giving the action a place in the town's trade.

Powder does not settle a doubtful name

Grinding keeps the ingredient's quality and history. It also keeps what you believe about it. A plant you only know by a folk name does not suddenly introduce itself because it has become powder.

The bag keeps dried and crushed parts under the name you know, with separate rows for their preparation. One part becoming powder does not multiply the contents or quietly identify the rest.

Room for what you make

If the remaining dried parts and the new powder will not both fit, the action leaves the specimen alone. It gives no practice for an attempt that produced nothing. Grinding the last part can reuse the space it leaves behind.

Returning to Oakwell keeps both the prepared ingredient and the practice earned from making it. They belong to the same saved character.

This pass brings the mortar action into the playable town. Drying racks, broader preparation and the profession controls still have their own work ahead.

item.title: A field book you can correct
item.description: A road note is useful until you learn something better. Perhaps the ford is deeper than it looked, or the bridge is the safer way home. The county field book now lets you correct your own words.
item.content:encoded:
A field book you can correct

A road note is useful until you learn something better. Perhaps the ford is deeper than it looked, or the bridge is the safer way home. The county field book now lets you correct your own words.

Open the map and choose a note from the list along the foot of the page. Edit changes its wording while keeping the pin where you put it. Erase removes that annotation and frees space for another. The drawing itself still belongs to the character's observations.

Copies keep their own history

A field copy is its own sheet. Correcting a warning on one copy does not quietly rewrite the original book, and erasing it does not remove the same warning from another page. You can leave an old description in the book while making a copy with better directions.

The changes travel with the saved county journey. Returning to the road keeps both corrected wording and deliberate erasures. Cancelling a note leaves the page as it was.

This is a small addition to the existing county exploration view. The larger work of carrying, studying and trading physical maps is still ahead. For now, it makes the notes already on the page something you can live with and revise as the journey teaches you more.

item.title: Where the reeds grow
item.description: A fishing town should begin before its first house. The approach ought to tell you where the water is: upright reeds in broken groups, a lower grassy bank, then the open space where boats land and people work.
item.content:encoded:
Where the reeds grow

31 October 2026

A fishing town should begin before its first house. The approach ought to tell you where the water is: upright reeds in broken groups, a lower grassy bank, then the open space where boats land and people work.

This pass gives the county a first layer of that shoreline character. The planting reads the real lake edge and river shape, so it can gather along a bend rather than follow the edge of a field or a scenery window. The same place keeps the same plants when the view moves.

Room beside the water

The first additions are dry-bank rushes and reeds. They use the existing ground and clearance rules, leaving roads, cultivated land and occupied features clear. Open water keeps its own rules. A plant's closeness to a lake does not mean it can stand in the lake, or that a boat can float beside it.

The groups need gaps. A solid fringe would hide the waterline and make every bank feel fenced off. Broken patches leave room to approach the water, with lower grass and exposed wet earth between the colonies.

The bank needed more than reeds

The first comparison exposed a bigger problem. Bright meadow grass ran straight to a dark cut edge, and the lake wore the same busy white foam as moving water. Adding upright plants could not hide that.

The graphical pass gives the bank a damp, broken margin. Dark runnels spread through patches of earth and low grey shingle. Stranded twigs and smaller satellite plants break up the repeated clumps. Reeds have separate stems, arched leaves, dry blades and occasional brown seed heads. The inland floor gradually returns to its original meadow or woodland colours.

The water needed another pass. Looking at the beach made the missing layers clear: wet ground beneath a thin reflective film, a visible shallow bed, then deeper colour where the bottom falls away. A flat opaque surface could not give us that edge.

The lake and brook now have a separate submerged bed beneath transmitting water. Silt tongues break up the shallows, while reflected light and small broken lapping crests soften the bank. The bed darkens through blue-green as it deepens. The dry ground keeps its walking height, and the water keeps its existing physical outline.

These are views from the production scenery renderer, captured headlessly with matching cameras and light. They are not native gameplay captures.

Towards a waterfront town

Reedhythe, the fishing town's working name, already has a first plan with a quay, jetties, fish market and boatyard. Its next pass needs to grow from the shore itself: a supported landing near the water, a busy working quay, then narrow homes climbing behind stone walls and stairs.

The new scenery is a foundation for that work. Natural banks should carry the planting; the landing, boat slip and market routes need open working space. Slate, timber and stone should have different jobs in the silhouette, from the low open boat shed to the taller homes above it.

There is still a town to refine. This pass does not finish its waterfront, animate its boats or settle the final reference comparison. It gives the surrounding land a clearer identity and records the rules the next town pass will need to follow.

item.title: When the roofs fill
item.description: Heavy rain should change the small life of a town. Sparrows leave the open ground, rats stop crossing the lanes, and a cat finds somewhere to wait. When the weather clears, those same animals should come back out.
item.content:encoded:
When the roofs fill

31 October 2026

Heavy rain should change the small life of a town. Sparrows leave the open ground, rats stop crossing the lanes, and a cat finds somewhere to wait. When the weather clears, those same animals should come back out.

This pass starts in Kilnworth with five sparrows, two rats and two cats. They are the existing ambient population, with their own positions and habits. The storm interrupts those habits and sends them towards reachable roof cover.

A place to wait

The animals read the same weather as the people and the rain on screen. Light rain lets them carry on. Thunder or a downpour sends them looking for shelter, with a short individual delay so the whole street does not turn at once.

A roof has to be real. Standing beside a wall can give a rat a hiding place, but it does not necessarily keep anything dry. The new shelter choices come from the town's actual roofed spaces. The animals still have to reach them through the same ground and walls that shape the town.

A blocked route leaves an animal where it really is. It can try again; it cannot disappear from the lane and reappear indoors. Birds and cats remain beneath the roof, with the scenery hiding them where it should. Rats keep their existing rule that hiding requires a proper hiding place.

One early version let several animals stop at the first edge of a roof. They now continue to their assigned places beneath it. It is a small change that makes waiting together easier to read.

The lull before they leave

A brief break in the rain is not enough. The animals wait for at least six continuously safe seconds, then release their shelter routines at slightly different times. Renewed bad weather resets that wait. When they leave, ordinary wandering, pecking and chasing resume.

A refuge also has to stay safe. The underlying animal rules let a nearby hazard interrupt shelter and take priority over waiting for the sky. Fire escape is covered by simulation checks; connecting the traced town's own fire hazards to this first population remains separate work.

One inhabited corner

This is a bounded first population on Kilnworth's ground floor. Its individuals stay attached to that place while the town replaces the scenery textures around the view. That replacement must update how they sit behind walls and roofs without moving or replacing the animals themselves.

There is more to do: wildlife on other levels, animals beyond the town, and weather arriving from the regional climate and seasons. This pass gives one corner of town a reason to empty in the rain and fill again afterwards. The native tour checks that first slice from rain to recovery; the wider wildlife work remains open.

item.title: When the crate breaks
item.description: A crate of apples makes a small promise. Its slats hold something. That red heap belongs to someone, and a hard enough blow ought to leave apples on the cobbles.
item.content:encoded:
When the crate breaks

31 October 2026

A crate of apples makes a small promise. Its slats hold something. That red heap belongs to someone, and a hard enough blow ought to leave apples on the cobbles.

Oakwell's market has been full of those promises. Crates, barrels and sacks helped make the square look busy, but they were scenery. This pass gives its reserve goods a physical life: a container can take damage, break apart and leave its actual contents behind.

This first pass covers twelve street reserves in Oakwell. Bringing the same rules to counter displays and other towns is still ahead.

A deliberate mess

Stand close to a container and its prompt names the owner, the container and its remaining integrity. Press K to strike it. An ordinary crate takes two accepted blows; a barrel holds together a little longer. The first blow leaves a visible crack. The breaking blow replaces the container with its wreckage and spills its finite stock.

This is a deliberate action, with a swing and a contact point. You have to reach the goods from the same ground. Standing upstairs, behind a wall or on the far side of another solid counter is not enough.

The broken material remains readable. Wooden containers leave lengths of timber, wicker breaks into lighter pieces, and a sack becomes a slack patch of cloth. Their old obstruction goes too. The place where the crate stood becomes ground you can walk across.

What falls out

The reserve stock follows the trade around it. Fruit, bread and folded cloth remain different things when they leave their containers. The spill has a repeatable pattern for that particular container, and round produce spreads farther than a loaf.

There is a practical limit to the mess. Goods need dry, supported ground. A proposed landing beneath a wall, in water or beyond a counter is replaced with a nearby clear place. If there is no safe room for the complete spill, the breaking blow cannot quietly destroy part of its contents.

Press E beside a fallen item to take it into the satchel, one item at a time. A full bag leaves it where it is. Apples on the ground do not become decoration again because there is nowhere to carry them.

These are the market's reserve and display goods. The merchant's trading menu still owns its separate counter stock; this pass does not pretend that smashing a reserve changes what the merchant is offering for sale.

The next visit remembers

The important part happens after the last apple lands. Break a crate, collect an apple, save and Continue: the crate must remain broken, the carried apple must remain in the bag, and the apples left outside must still be outside.

That whole state travels together. Returning to town cannot refill the same crate, and taking an item cannot save only half of its journey between ground and bag. An older visit gains the new intact reserves once, then carries their history forward.

The goods also keep their owner. Breaking them records whose container was damaged and what it held. Guard reactions, witnesses and restitution still need their own work; this square does not yet punish the player for vandalism.

For now, the change is small enough to understand with one broken crate. The market can lose something real. The player can leave a mess, walk through it, carry part of it away, and return to find the rest.

item.title: Following your hand
item.description: A quick click chooses a destination. Holding the pointer gives the next step back to your hand.
item.content:encoded:
Following your hand

31 October 2026

A quick click chooses a destination. Holding the pointer gives the next step back to your hand.

Walking around Oakwell has two different needs. Sometimes you want to point across the square and let the character find a way there. Sometimes you want to thread a doorway, follow a wall, or change your mind halfway through a step.

This pass keeps quick click-to-walk and adds continuous steering from a sustained left press. After a short hold, the character follows the pointer's current ground position. Move the pointer and the heading changes. Release and the held walk stops.

The walls still get a say

Steering asks the existing movement rules for a step. It does not move the character directly to a cursor position. Walls, doorways, stairs and water still decide where that step can go, and the existing collision slide lets a diagonal approach carry you along an obstacle.

The held walk also avoids asking for a new long route every frame. Choosing a destination remains a route-finding job; guiding the next step is a local movement job. Both end at the same physical rules.

Look where the spell is going

Mouse movement can turn the character towards the pointer. A right-click cast uses that direction immediately, so a quick change of aim does not wait for the next movement update. Keyboard walking remains available, and touch keeps its existing controls.

The fiddly part was deciding when your hand should stop owning the walk. A conversation, a menu or lost application focus cancels a held gesture. That includes the clock's small dawn-and-dusk menu. Closing a panel or finishing a wait while the button is still down does not send the character wandering off. You release and press again.

Opening the clock with the keyboard is a quiet action: its menu takes the key and leaves your aether alone. Waiting begins when you choose a time.

Clicks on people and interface controls keep their existing purpose. The aim is a movement option that fits the town's interactions, rather than another control competing with them.

A small loop worth testing properly

The native checks exercise a short route click, a held walk, a live reversal, release, keyboard movement, an actual ability panel, focus changes, a pointer-directed cast and sliding beside a wall. Separate simulation checks cover gesture timing and cancellation.

This work changes control and intent. It does not claim a new animation set or a measured frame-rate improvement. Its success is more immediate: the character should take the step you are asking for, and stop when you let go.

item.title: A workable seam
item.description: A walk beyond Oakwell can now bring back something the town can use. A standing rock, a mining pick, and a little room in your satchel are enough to begin.
item.content:encoded:
A workable seam

A walk beyond Oakwell can now bring back something the town can use. A standing rock, a mining pick, and a little room in your satchel are enough to begin.

Wenna has a pick to sell. Take it through the south gate to the pasture's outcrops and work a reachable face. The first blow can uncover a copper stain, a dark iron seam or a pale edge of quartz. Rough stone goes into the same satchel as everything else you carry.

There is only so much workable material in each rock. Its contents belong to that place in the seeded world, and the marks remain when you leave. Returning after quitting does not renew the reserve. A spent outcrop keeps its firm base; the hillside, the wall beside it and the way through the pasture stay where they were.

A full bag leaves the rock alone. You need room for the whole strike's stone and mineral before either is taken. That makes a return trip useful: sell the material to Wenna, or put actual iron ore toward one of the town's supply orders, and come back ready to work.

This is the first surface-quarrying pass in the playable town. The pick has a visible swing, but its weight and hand contact still need work. Prospecting, worn tools and digging into the land are ahead. For now, a small part of the country has become a place to work, with something finite to find and something useful to bring home.

item.title: A town with something on its mind
item.description: A smith can walk to work every morning and still feel like scenery. You need some way to learn what the work means to him: whether he expects to be paid, whether the forge has supplies, whether someone helped when it ran short.
item.content:encoded:
A town with something on its mind

31 October 2026

A smith can walk to work every morning and still feel like scenery. You need some way to learn what the work means to him: whether he expects to be paid, whether the forge has supplies, whether someone helped when it ran short. Today's work gives Oakwell's existing lives more ways to reach the player.

The first conversation now offers a short account of the person's day and a few things on their mind. Asking further opens a larger thought card. A comfort carries a plus, a worry a minus, and an ordinary concern a quiet dot. Hunger, friendship, unpaid wages and learning a trade can sit beside one another. These are named concerns, with a little explanation, rather than a single happiness number.

A name still needs an introduction. Meeting a stranger does not hand over everyone they know or every accusation in their history. The words come from things that person can express, with unfamiliar people kept unfamiliar.

There are also voices for all fourteen kinds of decision the villagers already make: work, asking for help, practice, theft, fighting, defiance, searching, posting a notice, friendship, departure, quitting, retraining, founding a venture and courtship. A failed attempt has its own words. The street example in this recorded visit is an ordinary day's work; the wider set is checked in the simulation. Hearing a choice depends on being near the actual person, with no wall between you.

One useful failure came from reading quietly. An early engine check found that the catch journal could react behind the thought card. The card now contains those world shortcuts while you read, while its own buttons keep their ordinary keyboard and touch controls. Reading also leaves the conversation's accumulated practice alone.

The visit being recorded is staged: the player starts on legal ground near the smith, the clock is held for inspection, and one piece of ore is supplied. The request itself comes from the working town. Delivering that ore uses the ordinary conversation: it leaves the satchel, reaches the workshop and earns payment from the request's finite funds.

Coming back gives that small transaction a human consequence. The smith recognises the traveller who brought the ore. The expanded card carries the same help as a remembered comfort. Quitting and continuing in a fresh process preserves that exact deed. The traveller walks back to the forge, finds the smith at his work, and hears the same recognition.

Some consequences belong in the street. Small public placards describe the authored forge, herb garden and inn as open, closed, waiting for supplies or behind on wages. A sentence can put an anonymous paper notice at the town's existing public anchor. These notes do not create a new building or a set of solid stocks. A newly founded venture still needs a real place before it can acquire scenery.

The remaining question belongs to a player: after twenty minutes here, can you tell someone what happened to these people, and why? That is the review this work is preparing for.

item.title: A name before a remedy
item.description: A traveller's herb bag should remember what they have learned, including the things they have learned incorrectly.
item.content:encoded:
A name before a remedy

31 October 2026

A traveller's herb bag should remember what they have learned, including the things they have learned incorrectly.

Pick a plant you have never met and the bag has a choice to make. It can tell you the answer, or it can help you keep track of the question. This pass gives Oakwell the second kind of bag.

The player begins with a folded linen pouch. Gathered leaves and flowers stay real carried specimens, alongside the things bought from a trader. Opening the pouch sorts them into headings based on what the character knows. Parts, preparations and observations sit underneath. The pouch uses the existing satchel space; it adds organisation rather than extra capacity.

A name you would actually give it

An unfamiliar hairy plant might become a fuzzy-leaved weed or a tall nettly thing. Those little names are seeded for the character, so returning to a save does not rename everything. Two plants that look the same remain together until there is a reason to distinguish them.

That matters most when one of them is a lookalike. A tidy list of separate species would quietly give the game away. The underlying specimens still carry their real identity for the simulation. The bag's headings, descriptions and ordinary unknown-item icons cannot use that hidden answer.

Experience without certainty

Examining a specimen offers a separate choice to taste one part. It consumes that part and records sensations: bitter, watery, peppery, or an unsettled stomach. Tasting does not turn an unfamiliar plant into a certain identification.

The observation belongs to the specimen that was tried. During review, we found that the older inventory rules could combine nearby plants into one physical stack. That would let an observation bleed into another plant's history. Newly gathered specimens now keep their separate provenance, even when the pouch presents them together.

A herbalist can still offer a name, and an uncertain opinion remains an opinion. The bag can move a specimen under a named heading without rewriting what it really is.

Out of the menu and into the garden

The first gathering places are small authored patches beside Oakwell's public garden. Reach, walls, available leaves and flowers, and satchel space all matter. Picking leaves the roots in place. A full bag leaves the plant where it is.

The visit also exposed a small fault in the garden itself. A resident could reach a bench and keep shuffling beside it, because the final approach was closer to the seat than their body could fit. That last step now gives them enough room to sit.

Checks against older saves caught another detail: the new herb records were changing the saved form of older dropped specimens. Existing drops now keep their original format and contents. New discoveries should not disturb belongings already left in the world.

The new records travel with the existing town save: what was gathered, what remains on the plant, what was tasted, and whether the starting pouch has already been issued. Loading again must preserve the visit rather than supply another pouch or refill a picked plant.

This is a first usable town slice. Wider plant distribution, deeper preparation work and more ways to notice a plant's effects can build on it. The useful part is already a small adventure: find something, give it a name, keep a sample, and decide whether to trust what you think you know.

item.title: What you leave behind
item.description: Put a feather down in the square. Leave the game. Come back. It should still be your feather, in that square.
item.content:encoded:
What you leave behind

30 October 2026

Put a feather down in the square. Leave the game. Come back. It should still be your feather, in that square.

Oakwell already lets you buy from a travelling cart, carry supplies to a workshop and earn a companion's trust. Those small exchanges give its people a reason to be there. This piece of work gives the traveller a way to handle the things that make those exchanges possible.

The travel bag now opens in the playable town. Its sixteen pockets hold the same belongings that merchants see across their counters. Lift something, move it into another pocket, combine matching stacks or split a few pieces off for later. The leather, stitching and brass belong beside the rest of the town's instruments; the contents belong to the journey you are making.

Make room without throwing things away

Sometimes a full bag needs a practical answer. The bag offers a choice of putting down one item, half a stack or the whole thing. What leaves the pocket becomes a small visible pile in the world. Close the bag, move beside it and choose to pick it up again.

The pile waits where you left it. Walking nearby does not pull it toward you. If only part will fit, you take that part and the rest remains on the ground. A completely full bag leaves everything in place, with an explanation of why it cannot be picked up.

That sounds modest until there are stairs and rooms involved. An item upstairs belongs upstairs. A wall still separates the person from the thing on its other side. Putting something down halfway along a stair is refused, so it cannot end up between floors. The same physical rules that make the inn a place to walk through also matter to what you carry through it.

A specimen keeps its story

Some belongings contain more than a name and a number. An unfamiliar herb can carry a source, a condition and a judgement you have learned about it. Moving it to another pocket or putting it on the ground must preserve those details. A doubtful identification must remain doubtful when you pick the specimen up again.

Item use follows the actions the town already supports. The bag explains when something has no available use. It does not consume an antler merely because the traveller pressed a button, or quietly invent a new effect for an ordinary ingredient.

The return matters

The bag and the things on the ground are saved together. Returning restores both sides of the decision: the feather missing from its pocket and the feather waiting in the square. Picking it up then removes that pile as it returns to the bag.

This first pass belongs to Oakwell's existing saved community. Equipment, more item actions and a common character save across every town still need their own work. The useful foundation is here: belongings can occupy a real place, make room for another choice, and survive the player's return.

Sprawl has large creatures and distant places ahead of it. Giving a small possession a dependable place in the world is part of making those journeys feel worth taking.

item.title: A wall between voices
item.description: A conversation belongs on the same side of a wall as the person speaking. Making that rule cheaper should never make a closed room easier to overhear.
item.content:encoded:
A wall between voices

30 October 2026

A conversation belongs on the same side of a wall as the person speaking. Making that rule cheaper should never make a closed room easier to overhear.

The work behind a nearby voice

Oakwell repeatedly asks whether a wall stands between two points. The question helps decide which passing remarks reach you, whom you can talk to and which nearby objects you can interact with.

The answer used to require walking through the town's building walls and tall boundaries until something blocked the line. Most of those walls were nowhere near the conversation. A short exchange by a doorway still carried the cost of considering distant masonry.

The town now prepares a small spatial index of those fixed wall spans. A query first skips whole groups that cannot meet its line, then asks the original crossing rule about the remaining walls. It shares the existing collision hierarchy rather than introducing another world map.
