Keep the gaps, keep the walls

Doorways remain gaps. Low boundaries do not suddenly silence a voice. The inn's live walls still use their original scan, so changing one takes effect immediately. Replacing a town plan replaces its index, even when the town keeps the same name and seed.

Oblique wall spans retain their original scan alongside the index, while extremely tiny geometry uses the complete scan: floating-point rounding can give the historical rule an answer outside ordinary geometric bounds. The usual orthogonal town walls still use the index.

The awkward details matter too. A line ending exactly on a wall, a line running along one and a wall with no length must behave as before. The checks compare both directions separately rather than assuming that reversing a line always has the same answer.

More than three hundred thousand comparisons exercise generated settlement layouts and difficult geometry. Warmed queries create no managed garbage. Separate engine checks exercise the actual town's walls, replacement plans and live inn geometry.

What became cheaper

The measurement gives most queries to real doorways, with the remainder spread across the town's envelope. Each version receives exactly the same questions. The old scan and the index run in alternating order, and the record keeps every sample, including slower ones.

On the playable town's exported layout, the index avoids 98.3 percent of exact wall tests in that workload. Average exact tests fall from about thirty-eight per query to less than one. That leaves more of the town's repeated work out of the way without changing what a wall means.

The graph measures a small CPU operation on a shared machine. It does not establish a frame-rate gain, complete interaction latency or phone performance. This is a quieter improvement: the same boundaries, with less work each time the town needs to ask about them.

item.title: Choosing your fights
item.description: A wolf has teeth, fur and meat. A bandit has whatever they brought along. A guard has the authority to make a reckless afternoon end behind bars.
item.content:encoded:
Choosing your fights

30 October 2026

A wolf has teeth, fur and meat. A bandit has whatever they brought along. A guard has the authority to make a reckless afternoon end behind bars.

This first roadside combat slice gives those encounters different outcomes in Oakwell. A wolf and an armed bandit wait on reachable ground away from the market and its working land. Both warn before striking. Their warning stays where the blow is going to land, giving you time to step aside, guard or answer with a learned ability.

What is actually there

Winning does not put a reward straight into your pocket. The body remains where it fell. When the fighting is over, take a moment beside it to recover what is useful.

Skinning the wolf uses the existing butchery rules. A more capable hand can recover better parts; time and spoilage matter. There are no coins inside a wolf. Searching the bandit recovers their carried sword and small purse. If your bag cannot hold the whole transfer, it stays on the body for later.

A different sort of opponent

The road guard starts peacefully. Walking past is safe, and aiming at the nearest hostile does not quietly select the guard. Deliberately land a blow, though, and the guard has witnessed an assault against their own person.

Running far enough can end the immediate pursuit. It does not erase the offence. Yield nearby, or lose the fight, and the guard takes you into a small holding pen. Serve the short sentence or pay the fine from money you actually possess. Your belongings, searched bodies and outstanding offence share one saved history, so returning cannot refill a purse or make the guard forget.

This begins with one wolf, one bandit and one guard. A living network of camps, witnesses, bounties and prisons is still ahead. The first aim is smaller and playable: fighting should leave you with something tangible, and choosing the wrong fight should mean something too.

item.title: A life, written in rings
item.description: A walk through unfamiliar ground, a fish brought to the bank, a spell shaped in a fight: the things you do begin to gather around you.
item.content:encoded:
A life, written in rings

30 October 2026

A walk through unfamiliar ground, a fish brought to the bank, a spell shaped in a fight: the things you do begin to gather around you.

Sprawl already kept a record of what a character absorbed from their life. This update brings that growth into the playable town. Small motes rise from an act, circle the character, and settle inward. Their colours belong to the essence that was actually gained: a warm amber for work done with your hands, a cold blue for wonder, the familiar hues of the elements.

The motes stay dim and small enough to belong to the street. When a vessel is full, the excess glances away and scatters. The picture follows what the body could take in, including what it could not keep.

A ring around a life

A thin coloured ring now wraps the health vial. It fills clockwise as absorbed essence grows toward the next ring, carrying the colours of the experiences that made it. The count stays readable without filling the instruments with another experience total.

When a ring completes, the motes draw inward and a soft pulse marks the moment. Walking and the world carry on. A golden pip remembers points waiting to be placed; a small seed marks a talent still to choose.

Choosing what takes root

The ring opens a folio called Rings of a Life. Press F2, use the controller's View button, or tap the ring when you are safely out of a fight and on dry ground.

The five roots are Body, Hands, Guile, Word, and Mind. Each row shows the base, the points fixed by your life, the points you placed, and any contribution from talents. Free points are yours to spend. The folio records the choice and its new total.

Earned talent offers wait in the same place. Each card has a name and a description of what it changes. Choose one with a key, a controller, or a tap; the others in that offer fall away. Later offers remain waiting, and the talents already chosen stay listed below them.

These captures use a review character with accelerated earned progression, so the talent choice is visible. The decisions use the town's ordinary controls.

These are the existing body's progression choices, now available in the town. This update does not add a new combat scaling system to the five stat totals.

The road teaches too

Travel grows from time spent actually walking. Pressing against a wall earns no journey, and time spent in a panel adds no hidden walking practice. Partial progress survives Continue, so a short walk is still part of the next one.

The town also remembers first visits to small patches of ground, its actual grassland and woodland habitats, and nearby landmarks such as the old tree, shrines, bridges, and outlying workplaces. Reaching them gives wonder. The saved history keeps those discoveries remembered when you return.

This first integration belongs to the playable town and its outskirts. It does not claim that every place across the planned county can already be explored. It gives the places you can reach a lasting part in the character you are becoming.

item.title: The ground remembers
item.description: A firebolt is gone in a moment. The small dark trail it leaves tells a longer story.
item.content:encoded:
The ground remembers

29 October 2026

A firebolt is gone in a moment. The small dark trail it leaves tells a longer story.

Magic in Sprawl should belong to the place where it happens. This first pass gives fire and water a local aftermath in the playable town. A released fire spell leaves warm, scorched ground. The heat fades first; the blackened trace remains for a while, then wears away.

Another spell can answer it

Water cools a hot trace, briefly raises steam, and washes the scorch into a damp patch. Fire meeting already wet ground makes steam instead of silently burning through it. The marks follow the town's real walls and ground heights, so a spell does not leave a trail inside a house or on a floor beneath its path.

The aftermath comes from ordinary learned abilities. There is no extra button to remember, and it costs nothing beyond the spell already cast. Its damage and the player's movement remain governed by their existing rules.

Small lives notice

The town's ambient animals read the lingering heat. A cat resting nearby can get up and flee; birds and rats avoid hot ground too. Once the heat is gone, those routes become available again. A harmless old scorch does not keep frightening them.

The traces share the saved learning history. Returning does not restart their lifetimes, and waiting through part of the day lets them fade. The first implementation keeps only a small, bounded local history, with separate places and ground heights.

This begins with fire and water and the town's small wildlife. Weather washing traces away, companions making their own decisions around them, and consequences for more essences still lie ahead. The aim is to let a familiar spell leave a readable memory in a familiar place.

item.title: A plant with the wrong name
item.description: Wenna has brought a few dried plant specimens to market. Their names are uncertain. Ysolde can turn them over, name her price, and show you what makes one plant different from its lookalike.
item.content:encoded:
A plant with the wrong name

25 October 2026 · Day 34

Wenna has brought a few dried plant specimens to market. Their names are uncertain. Ysolde can turn them over, name her price, and show you what makes one plant different from its lookalike.

A real question for the herbalist

The town already had a herbalist, a herb garden and a question about identifying plants. That question now leads to a working service. Carry uncertain specimens to Ysolde and she offers an examination, with a fee you can accept or decline.

If you can settle the fee in coin, that payment goes into her actual purse. Otherwise she can keep one specimen from each batch for her trouble. The rest remain yours. Parts from the same source receive the same judgement, even when they are split between stacks in your bag.

The difference is in the tell

A familiar-looking leaf can belong to a different plant. Ysolde uses the knowledge earned through her years as a herbalist, and explains the distinguishing feature from the plant catalogue. Her skill makes her a useful person to seek out, while the existing possibility of a mistaken judgement remains part of the world.

Wenna's specimens are a finite introduction lot. Buying them does not make more appear when you return to the game. The labels, payment and remaining stock belong to the same saved town visit.

A small lesson that stays with the visit

The review follows an ordinary traveller through the town: walk to the cart, buy the specimens, find Ysolde, hear the price, decline, then ask again and pay. A second game process continues that same saved visit. The named specimens and both purses return as they were, while the cart remains sold out.

The conversation is also checked at a compact window size. Changing your mind keeps your money and specimens. An old offer cannot be used after its contents or payment have changed, and pressing the same confirmation twice cannot charge the fee again.

This is a first usable connection between the town's herb trade, its herbalist and the plants' existing lookalike rules. Learning outdoors and building a wider life around gathered plants can grow from that connection.

item.title: When night falls on the market town
item.description: Oakwell used to blink from the end of the market day straight into morning. Now the town keeps its own hours, and the player can stay out after sunset.
item.content:encoded:
When night falls on the market town

25 October 2026 · Day 34

Oakwell used to blink from the end of the market day straight into morning. Now the town keeps its own hours, and the player can stay out after sunset.

The long way to morning

The town clock no longer skips from dusk to dawn. Afternoon light warms toward evening, then a cool blue settles over the lanes. Deep night holds steady across midnight. As morning approaches, the darkness lifts into a warm sunrise before daylight returns.

A small clock in the corner shows the day and the time. In this town, a full day still passes in four minutes, so evening arrives quickly enough to watch in one visit. Midnight moves the village into its next day while the square remains dark.

The square closes

At dusk, Maud and Edric's fixed counters close and stand empty. A little moon sign marks each closed stall, and a traveller who approaches can see when it will reopen. At dawn, the stalls open again. The travelling pedlar keeps her own route around town.

The town's residents keep their own routines: finishing work, walking home, sleeping and returning to their daytime activities. You can watch those routines continue as the town grows dark.

A town that stays awake with you

Night is part of play now. You can cross the square after closing, watch the lamps come into their own, and see the town begin to wake again at dawn. The clock, the market and the residents all share the same passing hours. The images show a fixed market view at two review times in the game's own renderer.

item.title: The roads a town remembers
item.description: A town feels alive when its people can get on with their day. The smith leaves home, a neighbour finds the market, and someone trying to reach a closed-off courtyard gives up without making the rest of the simulation wait.
item.content:encoded:
The roads a town remembers

A town feels alive when its people can get on with their day. The smith leaves home, a neighbour finds the market, and someone trying to reach a closed-off courtyard gives up without making the rest of the simulation wait.

This update works beneath those journeys. Townsfolk already share a picture of where a person can stand. They now remember which patches of that ground actually join each other.

Learning the streets once

Previously, an impossible destination could make a route request search an entire connected neighbourhood before returning empty-handed. Every further request had to learn the same disappointing answer again.

The new router labels connected ground once when it is built. After the existing quick checks, a destination in a separate patch can be refused before the expensive search begins. Ordinary journeys keep their existing search order, corners, doorway rules and path smoothing. A straightforward walk across an open square keeps its quick path too.

Proving the change

More than 41,000 little journeys were compared with the previous router across every possible arrangement of a small test grid. Further checks covered generated towns, separate inn floors, narrow doors, blocked corners, isolated rooms and repeated requests. Successful routes keep exactly the same waypoints.

In a deliberately disconnected test landscape, a request previously inspected 31,744 cells before failing. It now inspects none in the search. Across five independent benchmark runs, the measured time per request fell from roughly 7.9 milliseconds to 0.013 milliseconds. These are measurements of the routing code outside the game engine; they do not establish a frame-rate improvement in play.

Ordinary successful routes measured essentially the same as before. Preparation has a price: around 440 KiB of additional memory per generated-town router in the test, and roughly one to one-and-a-half extra milliseconds to build it. That work is paid once, while townsfolk reuse the result throughout their day.

An earlier experiment also tried remembering every neighbouring step. It did not earn its extra complexity in the measurements, so the final change keeps the smaller connectivity improvement.

This work concerns townsfolk using the shared settlement router. Player click routes, terraced-town navigation and changes to the shape of the world have their own requirements.

item.title: Small lives, less work
item.description: A cat watching a rat and sparrows scattering across the square help a town feel inhabited. This update makes the work underneath those small lives cheaper, while keeping their movements and decisions the same.
item.content:encoded:
Small lives, less work

25 October 2026 · Day 34

A cat watching a rat and sparrows scattering across the square help a town feel inhabited. This update makes the work underneath those small lives cheaper, while keeping their movements and decisions the same.

The quiet work behind the square

The town's animals need to know where they can stand. Walls, the inn, market furniture and the well all matter. Before an animal takes its first step, the town prepares a fine map of solid ground around the square.

The earlier sampler could ask about each kind of obstacle at every little point. A large patch beneath a building kept asking questions whose answer was already clear. The new sampler marks those solid footprints first, then asks the town's existing collision rules about the remaining ground. The points being sampled and the clearance around masonry stay the same.

A short journey should ask a smaller question

Finding the start of an animal's route used to scan the entire reachable patch, even though the animal could only join a node within two units. It now considers the nearby cells in the same order. A route search stops when it has found the destination's existing path, instead of continuing across the rest of the square. Checking whether a rat has reached cover uses a direct lookup.

The animals still check the ground as they move. A new obstruction can still stop a step. Sparrows keep their flight from nearby people, rats keep their hiding places, and cats keep their short chases.

Keeping the same little lives

The previous implementation remains as a test reference. Both versions receive the same seed, people, changing obstructions and passage of time. Tests compare the complete animal state, including paths and random-generator state, rather than relying on a similar-looking final picture.

The comparison includes disconnected ground, narrow passages, negative coordinates, different window sizes and positions large enough to expose floating-point edge cases. The ground sampler has its own comparison: each sampled bit must agree with the original calculation.

What the measurements show

The collision-map comparison uses a previously captured town plan with declared street props. Preparing its 129,600 samples fell from 37.5 milliseconds to 7.5 milliseconds, while measured managed allocation fell from 37.9 megabytes to 0.13 megabytes. A generated town with additional synthetic props fell from 34.0 milliseconds to 5.1 milliseconds. The fixtures and shared-host limits are recorded with the measurements.

In a synthetic patch with the same 41-cell width as the town's wildlife window, 60,000 complete simulation steps fell from 324.0 milliseconds to 156.3 milliseconds. The same animals reached the same states, with zero managed allocation inside both tick loops. Larger windows benefited more from skipping distant cells.

Each comparison uses three fresh processes, alternating the original and optimized versions. The raw record keeps every sample and the slow outliers. The graph shows the median of the three process medians.

These measurements cover specific engine-free CPU workloads. Complete loading time, frame rate and device performance need separate native measurements. The practical gain is less repeated work beneath the town's existing small lives, with the rules that make them believable kept intact.

item.title: One vocation, many skills
item.description: A traveller can learn to gather useful plants without deciding that gathering is their life's work. A warrior can prepare a field remedy. An apothecary can still become a careful picker.
item.content:encoded:
One vocation, many skills

A traveller can learn to gather useful plants without deciding that gathering is their life's work. A warrior can prepare a field remedy. An apothecary can still become a careful picker. The profession work being recovered for review starts from that distinction: ordinary practice stays open, while a deliberately chosen vocation gives a character a deeper direction.

A choice that keeps its meaning

Letting a character collect every profession makes experimentation easy, but eventually gives every seasoned traveller the same collection of specialist techniques. Locking ordinary activities behind one profession creates a different problem: a person who chose another craft cannot do a simple useful task even after practising it.

The proposed middle ground is one major profession, with ordinary skills that keep growing through use. Trying an activity comes before committing. The character's combat abilities remain a separate choice. A profession is a direction to develop, rather than a replacement for the rest of the character.

That leaves room for trade to matter. Two capable travellers can share ordinary knowledge yet value each other's specialised products. Buying a carefully made remedy does not mean learning the method that produced it.

Start with the rules of a useful craft

The recovered foundation concentrates on the journey from plant to field remedy. Its rules model Herbalist and Apothecary as alternative major professions within that connected activity. Gathering and preparation can advance ordinary practice before choosing either one. This foundation is not yet connected to the current town's player controls.

The specialist choices aim to change actual production. A careful harvesting method can recover more usable material; a preservation method can help prepare still-viable aged ingredients. An apothecary can favour stronger remedies or more output from a preparation. A choice should describe its effect before it becomes permanent.

Practice needs to come from successful work. Reading a menu, reopening an offer, cancelling an attempt or loading a save must not advance a profession. Products also need to keep their actual properties when traded or saved, rather than changing because their maker later learned something new.

Recovering the unfinished work

This is work in review, not a released feature. The earlier branch was left without a pull request while the town and its character systems continued to change. Its old controls and save integration cannot simply be brought back alongside the newer systems. The first recovery increment isolates the profession and crafting rules so they can be checked without replacing today's character ownership.

The playable integration remains ahead. It must use the town's current inventory, money and character save transaction, work alongside the herbalist service already there, and give the profession menu a suitable control. A separate copy of a traveller's goods or health would make the craft unreliable, especially after returning to a saved game.

The design also has clear limits. This first craft does not make smithing, cooking or every other profession playable. It has authored specialist choices rather than an unlimited generator of new powers. Retraining is not part of the initial proposal, so the commitment needs a clear explanation before it is accepted.

The next review needs to show the full sequence in the town: gather, practise, choose, prepare, use and trade, then save and return. Those checks matter as much as the profession menu. The aim is a choice that makes a character distinctive throughout play, with ordinary competence still earned by doing the work.

item.title: Familiar roads
item.description: A smith walks from home to the forge. A neighbour heads for the market, then makes the same journey tomorrow. Town life is full of familiar routes, and finding each of them from scratch is work the town need not keep repeating.
item.content:encoded:
Familiar roads

A smith walks from home to the forge. A neighbour heads for the market, then makes the same journey tomorrow. Town life is full of familiar routes, and finding each of them from scratch is work the town need not keep repeating.

The latest change gives the town router a small shared memory. Once it has found a way around buildings, another request between the same patches of ground can reuse that search. Townsfolk already share the router, so the memory belongs to the neighbourhood rather than to one person.

Remember the way, keep the destination

A remembered route is a corridor through the ground, not somebody else's finished walk. Each request still uses its own exact starting position and destination. The existing smoothing runs again, preserving the way corners, doorways and the final approach are handled.

Two neighbours on different sides of the same patch still need their own approaches. Sharing the search should not send either one to the other's doorstep. Straightforward walks across open ground keep their quick path, and separate areas still fail their connectivity check without searching.

The memory keeps at most sixteen recently used corridors, each no longer than 1,024 cells. Its stored cell payload cannot exceed 64 KiB, and storage is created only when needed. Older entries make room for new ones. Each router owns the memory for its unchanged map; a freshly built router begins empty.

What the measurements show

The comparison checks the remembered routes against a frozen copy of the original router and measures complete requests, including smoothing. Across five independent runs, repeated routes through two generated towns took roughly 0.31 and 0.34 milliseconds instead of 1.03 milliseconds: about three times faster for those requests.

There is a trade-off. A workload cycling through twenty-four routes, more than the memory can hold, measured about three per cent slower. Open-ground and disconnected requests remained essentially unchanged. The checks also exercise eviction and the size limits.

These are routing measurements outside the game engine. They do not establish a frame-rate improvement or the proportion of real villagers whose routes will be reused. The benefit in a live town depends on how often its people ask for familiar journeys; that actual play pattern still needs measuring.

item.title: A lighter step through the inn
item.description: A busy inn should spend its time on the people inside it. This update makes its existing collision checks cheaper, keeping the same doors, stairs and places a person can stand.
item.content:encoded:
A lighter step through the inn

25 October 2026 · Day 34

A busy inn should spend its time on the people inside it. This update makes its existing collision checks cheaper, keeping the same doors, stairs and places a person can stand.

Hundreds of little walls

Sprawl's inn is built from connected wings, galleries and roof rooms. Its walls follow those shapes in many short pieces. The three versions measured for this update contain between 836 and 867 wall spans.

Walking checks those walls repeatedly. A longer movement is broken into small steps so a person cannot slip through a thin wall between frames. Townsfolk also need to learn which places are clear before planning their journeys. Those careful checks are useful, but calculating the distance to every wall piece costs time.

A question that is cheaper to answer

Most inn walls run straight across or straight up the plan. Before calculating the distance to one of those spans, the inn can ask whether its entire wall line is already too far away to touch.

If it is, the more expensive calculation can be skipped. Everything nearby still goes through the established collision test. Diagonal walls keep that test too. Doorway gaps, rounded wall ends, furniture and the two flights of stairs retain their existing rules.

There is no stored copy of the walls to go stale. The check reads the current geometry every time, so a changed wall is seen on the next query.

Same footsteps, less work

The comparison runs the previous and updated movement code over the same inn geometry. It checks exact positions after movement, stair landings, narrow clearance, wall ends and changes to the walls while the inn stays open. Further checks probe the tiny numerical differences on either side of a collision boundary.

The measurements cover complete short movements and a grid of places a town route planner might sample. They measure the collision code outside the game engine. They do not establish an overall frame-rate improvement or a result on a phone.

Across three fresh benchmark processes, complete short movements used roughly 40–49% less CPU time in these samples. Sampling places a route planner might use took roughly 34–50% less. Both implementations produced the same checksums and allocated no managed memory inside the measured queries. The host was shared with other work, so the raw samples and their variation are retained.

This is a small change in the work each footstep asks the computer to do. The benefit comes from how often the inn asks the same kind of question.
